newsitem.title: PERU: Victorious Peru clamps down on assault criticism.
newsitem.headline: Victorious Peru clamps down on assault criticism.

text.p: Peru sought on Monday to capitalise on its successful military strike against Marxist rebel hostage-takers and quash lingering criticism of human rights abuses in the raid and its aftermath.

"Everyone has applauded the government's decision and the way 72 people were rescued so cleanly and professionally," Justice Minister Carlos Hermoza Moya said. "We must not question the ever-so-clean and so beautiful way in which our men (soldiers) have given up their lives ... to save the highly valuable lives of 72 hostages."

Despite the death of one captive -- Judge Carlos Giusti, who bled to death after the attack -- the government claims the rescue achieved its goal because all 72 hostages were freed alive from the Japanese ambassador's residence.

Hermoza was the latest in a line of senior officials, including President Alberto Fujimori, to reject claims that two rebels were captured and executed during the raid and that families were kept away from the rebels' bodies afterward.

Those reports have threatened to tarnish the world acclaim Peru had received for the military strike, hailed as one of the great rescue operations. All 14 Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels and two commandos were slain on Tuesday when 140 commandos exploded through walls and tunnels to end Latin America's longest hostage siege.
Hermoza rejected demands from the influential Lima chamber of lawyers for an investigation into why Giusti's life was not saved with the application of a tourniquet.

While the military was reviewing its strategy to flush out the approximately 200 remaining MRTA fighters in Peru's remote eastern jungle zone, the government moved to silence the group's international spokesman, Isaac Velazco, who is based in Hamburg, Germany, local media reported.

Velazco, whose public statements and maintenance of an MRTA Internet website constantly irritated the government during the four-month crisis, has been threatening reprisals from the MRTA to avenge Tuesday's attack.

The German government on Monday called on the government of Hamburg to ban his political activity following reports that Peru's Foreign Ministry had formally requested a cancellation of his political asylum status.
"I don't understand how there are countries who put up with these individuals who from abroad perform a role so disastrous to Peru," Hermoza said.

Fujimori, buoyed by soaring popularity and plaudits for the raid, continued on Monday a series of triumphant public appearances and media interviews. "There are some things we Peruvians can do better than the U.S. ... Compare this with Waco," Fujimori said in an interview with Time magazine.

On Monday, he attended the inauguration with Thor Heyerdahl of an expedition depicting the Norwegian explorer's epic 1947 voyage that crossed the Pacific. Then he paid a visit to the Vatican's office in Peru, where he thanked the Roman Catholic Church for its support in the crisis.

He dismissed rumours that the Vatican's representative on a three-man guarantors' committee overseeing negotiations -- Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani -- had aided the government by sneaking monitoring devices into the house. A captive retired navyman tipped off troops to the right moment for the bloody attack via a microphone planted in a crucifix.
But Fujimori said: "I thoroughly reject those who seek to involve Monsignor Cipriani, and the other members of the guarantors' commission, or the medical team in this work.
"This is the exclusive responsibility of my government and that is under my responsibility ... we had sufficient information from outside and from the tunnels with our own technology."
